description: A tall, straight pine with a clear trunk, thick bark broken into cinnamon-orange plates between black fissures, and long needles (12-25 cm, in threes) in tufts at the branch tips; 22-38 m tall here. It grows above the oak woodland in the lower conifer forest, from about 600 m up, and its thick bark lets old trees survive the frequent low fires that once kept these forests open.

season_notes.winter: Evergreen: needles stay on for about three years, so the crown is full in every season.
season_notes.spring: Pollen cones release clouds of yellow pollen (May-June) and new shoots extend at the branch tips.
season_notes.summer: Second-year seed cones grow to full size and turn from green to red-brown.
season_notes.fall: Cones open and drop winged seeds (September-October) for squirrels, chipmunks and birds; the oldest needles yellow and fall.

notes: The dominant pine of the lower montane conifer forest above the foothills. Mature trees here 22-38 m (to 70 m elsewhere), dbh 0.6-1.2 m (dbh/height about 0.03), with a tall, straight, barely tapering trunk clear of branches for nearly half its height (bole_ratio and base_size 0.45; lower limbs self-prune). Excurrent Rauh's model: the leader runs to the top (length_ratio 1, taper 1) and level-1 branches are whorled (about three per visible whorl in old trees), roughly horizontal: the lowest droop slightly below horizontal (98 degrees) and arch down and turn up again at the tips (droop_deg 34 over the inner half, upturn_deg 40 over the outer half, because in-world review found the limbs too straight), the upper ones ascend (58 degrees). Old crowns are open, narrowly rounded to flat-topped, hence the tapered_cylindrical shape (long branches persist near the top). Bark of mature 'yellow pine' is the signature: thick cinnamon-orange plates separated by deep black fissures ('plates' pattern); young trees ('blackjacks') are dark. Needles 12-25 cm in bundles of three, dark yellow-green, held in dense brush-like tufts at the ends of the twigs, so level-2 twigs carry only foliage (near_sides 0) and cards are needle_cluster tufts aligned with the twig.
sources: Oliver and Ryker 1990, Silvics of North America vol. 1, Pinus ponderosa
Halle, Oldeman and Tomlinson 1978 (Rauh's model; Pinus as example)
